cards.heading: Three-tier definition
cards.question: What are the three tiers of layered agent memory?
cards.answer: Short-term session memory (current task state, recent tool outputs); long-term memory (typically a vector store, cross-session context and learned patterns); structured logs (a durable audit/debugging record).

cards.heading: Failure it prevents
cards.question: What design failure does layered agent memory exist to prevent?
cards.answer: Designing an agent like a chatbot — just passing the conversation in and taking a response out — which makes context-window overflow a production incident rather than a design parameter.

cards.heading: Why one transcript fails
cards.question: Why does a single conversation transcript fail as an agent's only memory on long tasks?
cards.answer: It forces one retention policy on three needs with incompatible lifetimes: high-detail short-lived task state crowds out working room, while the durable record that should survive vanishes with the session.

cards.heading: Structured logs are distinct
cards.question: What makes the structured-logs tier different from the session and long-term tiers?
cards.answer: It must survive whatever the agent chooses to forget, and unlike the other two tiers it is never consumed by the model at all — it exists for people to inspect after the fact.

cards.heading: Retrofit cost
cards.question: Why is retrofitting layered memory onto an already-deployed agent risky?
cards.answer: It usually amounts to a partial rebuild, because the tier boundaries determine what the agent was ever able to record — so the design decision is front-loaded, not deferrable.
